title: Inquest provides relief ; Family of Ottawa man killed by OPP want officers to get better training
article: Phillip Jeffrey Charbonneau's loved ones are looking for closure after the inquest into his death ended Thursday.
Charbonneau, an Ottawa man killed by OPP officers in July 2009, was shot in the head after he attempted to flee a roadblock near the Cedar Valley Golf and Country Club.
For almost two weeks, Charbonneau's family has sat through an inquest that revealed graphic details about his death.
"They mentioned what he looked like after he was shot and I couldn't handle that," said Taylor Bogden, Charbonneau's 17-year-old daughter.
"I just couldn't believe that there were six guys going against him. Where did they think he was going with two flat tires? This didn't need to happen," she said.

Bogden insists she understands her father did something wrong that night by attempting to flee a roadblock. But her unhappiness is directed toward what she believes is insufficient training that led to officers mishandling the situation.
"They said that they were in the wrong spot at the wrong time," said Bogden. "Police said in open court, 'I didn't know what to do.' I don't want that to be an answer."
When Bogden met the officer who forensics believe is responsible for her father's death, she felt pity and much of her anger and resentment toward him diminished.
"I could see that he felt sorry and that he understands what he did. I brought him to tears, he was very emotional," she said.
"I wanted to ease him from any suffering or torment he felt after the fact. He doesn't need to bring that home to his family."
She said no family will have to suffer if training improves.
Her sister, 13-year-old Jamie Bogden, said attending the inquest has been therapeutic and crucial to her healing process.

"We came here for answers and for the police officers to see what we saw in him," she said. "He won't walk us down the aisle, he won't be at our graduation. I just don't want anyone else to go through that."
Jessica Monette, Charbonneau's spouse, describes feeling some relief following the inquest.
"OPP lawyers were saying it could be an act of suicide because he was pushing them, but there was too much evidence against it," she said.
"I'm glad they classified it as a homicide even though the officers aren't necessarily being charged and I'm happy with some of the recommendations."
The recommendations by the jury after hearing include instruction to both the provincial government and the OPP.
